label: rem:three-euler-characteristics
title: The three Euler characteristics, and the trace that is not one
html:
Remark. The three Euler characteristics, and the trace that is not one

Four quantities in this paper have at one time or another been written \chi, and only two of them are Euler characteristics. They are kept apart by name, and this remark says what each one is, what it depends on, and what it equals for Bring's surface.

The topological Euler characteristic \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0) of the base curve is the alternating sum of its Betti numbers: for a closed orientable surface of genus g, \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0) = 2 - 2g. It is the integer that the Descartes condition fixes, through the genus: g(M_0) = 4, so \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0) = -6 (Euler characteristic of Bring's surface). Every downstream use of the number -6 — the count of torus-knot generators, the Hurwitz bound, the genus-ideal filtration, the Kummer divisibility n \mid 6 — consumes the genus, and this is the quantity it consumes. It has a Hochschild reading: by the Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg theorem the Hochschild homology of a smooth curve is HH_n(M_0) = \bigoplus_i H^i(M_0, \Omega^{i+n}), so \dim HH_0 = 2, \dim HH_1 = \dim HH_{-1} = g, and the alternating sum \sum_n (-1)^n \dim HH_n(M_0) = 2 - 2g is \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0) again.

The sheaf Euler characteristic \chi(M_0, V) = h^0(M_0, V) - h^1(M_0, V) of a vector bundle V on the base always carries two arguments. By Riemann–Roch (Chern character and Riemann–Roch) it equals \deg V + \operatorname{rk} V \cdot (1 - g), so it depends on the bundle, and it coincides with \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0) exactly when \deg V = (2 - \operatorname{rk} V)(1 - g) — for example for a degree-zero bundle of rank two, which is the case of the state bundle. It is the Euler characteristic of a cohomology, not of a space.

The quantum dimension \dim_q(X) = \mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{id}_X) \in \operatorname{End}(\mathbf{1}) of an object X of a rigid monoidal category is a trace, not an Euler characteristic. For the fundamental object V of \mathrm{SU}_q(2) it is [2]_q = q + q^{-1}, positive and q-dependent. For the Frobenius–Hopf object A the Peter–Weyl sum \sum_{m \geq 1} [m]_q^2 diverges at every real q > 1, and what one writes for \dim_q(A) depends on a regularisation (regular representation); no regularisation gives -6 at the substrate parameter. Writing \mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{id}_A) = -6 identifies a trace with a topological Euler characteristic; the two are different objects, and the equation is a collision of names rather than a theorem.

The obstruction class w(A) of the Wigner axiom is the fourth object. It lives in the classical-limit obstruction space, is a class rather than a number, and becomes an integer only through its archimedean image, the Euler class e(TM_0) \in H^2(M_0; \mathbb{Z}), whose integral is once more \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0). That the obstruction space is a line is the axiom, not a consequence of the axioms of a quantum observable universe.

The rule that follows from the table is the one the notation register now enforces: a bare \chi(A) does not occur; an Euler characteristic carries either the roman subscript \mathrm{eu} or two arguments; a trace is written \mathrm{tr} or \dim_q.
